hook.text: An Uber driver with a 4.3 rating earns 40% less than one with 4.8. Tenths of a point change lives.

buildup.text: Platform economies turned reputation into a number. Your score determines access to work and housing.

discovery.text: Airbnb hosts with African-American names get 16% fewer bookings. Bias hides inside 'objective' ratings.

twist.text: We escaped village gossip only to build global gossip systems with even less accountability.

climax.text: A bad review on Google can bankrupt a small business overnight—digital honor is economic survival.

punchline.text: Stars replaced whispers, but the power is the same.

quiz.question: What Airbnb study revealed racial bias in ratings and bookings?

details.summary: Online reputation scores — from Yelp ratings to LinkedIn endorsements to Uber stars — have created a universal honor system for the digital age. Your number determines your access to services, jobs, and social credibility. A low score is modern ostracism; a perfect score is modern honor.
details.whyItMatters: Online reputation scores are the digital equivalent of village gossip — decentralized, persistent, and consequential. They reveal that honor systems are not relics but evolving features of human social organization.
takeaways: Uber drivers below 4.6 stars face deactivation
Airbnb hosts and guests mutually rate each other's 'honor'
Online reputation cannot be reset — digital shame is permanent

faq.question: Are rating systems a form of honor culture?
faq.answer: Yes. Rating systems create reputational consequences for behavior — exactly what honor cultures do. High ratings confer trust and access (honor). Low ratings restrict opportunities and signal untrustworthiness (shame).

faq.question: What are the problems with digital reputation systems?
faq.answer: Rating systems can be manipulated (fake reviews), biased (racial discrimination in Airbnb ratings), and disproportionate (one bad interaction tanks an average). They create anxiety about performance that mirrors honor-culture stress.
